foundation.statement: Architecture practices rarely choose poorly. They choose reactively, without a coherent framework, and then live with the consequences compounding across years. The real problem is structural, not technical.

hero.heading: A clearer view of how your practice really works.
hero.lede: I’m Allister Lewis, an architect and technology strategist. I founded ADDD to help architecture leaders understand what is really holding their practice back—across technology, workflows, information, costs and decision-making.

perspective.heading: What Allister sees
perspective.lede: An external eye finds what internal teams have learned to live with.

tiles.text: Every practice has them. Manual steps inserted between tools. Data re-entered because systems do not talk. Email used as workflow because nothing else fits. These are not inefficiencies. They are invisible infrastructure. No one reports them because everyone assumes they are normal. An external review makes them visible and shows what becomes possible when they are removed.
tiles.title: Workarounds that became the system

tiles.text: One team picks software for speed. Another chooses based on cost. A third inherits legacy systems no one wants to replace. Each decision made sense at the time. Together they create governance gaps, duplicated data, conflicting workflows and costs that climb without visibility. The problem is not the tools. It is the absence of a framework that connects them.
tiles.title: Fragmented choices that compound into risk

tiles.text: Partners assume BIM is embedded. Project directors know it is partial. Teams use workarounds leadership has never seen. Investment in training does not translate to adoption. What gets reported upwards and what happens on projects are often two different stories. Closing that gap is where real change begins.
tiles.title: The gap between what leadership believes and what actually happens

validation.heading: Proven outcomes across architecture practices
validation.text: ADAM Architecture reduced licensing costs by half, uncovered eighteen hidden workflow steps and aligned leadership around a shared digital roadmap. The approach works because it treats technology as a system, not a series of isolated tools. Allister’s work spans 1,800+ researched AEC software solutions, direct experience with AJ100 practices and ongoing industry research through reports, speaking and the ADDDitive newsletter.

body: ## What it involves

Your company is named as the sponsor across ADDD’s workflow sessions and Technology Blueprint sessions for twelve months, and takes a slot in the ADDDitive newsletter every month. Within your category, you are the only sponsor.
Before anything is published, a tracked trial link is agreed and set up, so interest that comes through ADDD’s audience can be followed back to it. Reporting on that link arrives every month.
## Who it is for

It suits infrastructure, hardware, licensing, managed service and cloud providers: companies whose products support how practices work, rather than being the subject of ADDD’s editorial coverage. Design-tool vendors are usually better served by a featured workflow episode, which shows a tool inside a real project.
## How it stays independent
The sponsorship is always disclosed. Sponsors do not preview editorial content, and the sponsorship does not buy inclusion in recommendations, rankings or reviews, or a place in the ADDD Stack.
items.lede: A year-long sponsorship of ADDD’s workflow content and Technology Blueprint sessions, for companies that want to stay in front of architects and practice leaders over time rather than for a single moment.

body: ## How an episode is made
Every episode starts from a piece of architectural work, not from a product. The project is chosen with you and the practice involved, and needs a clear design or delivery problem worth explaining.

The architects and specialists who carried out the work explain their roles and decisions. The workflow is traced step by step: the inputs, the tools at each stage and how information moved between them. Only then does the episode turn to the role your technology played, what it was used for and why it suited the task.
## What is produced
An 8–10 minute workflow video, with a LinkedIn post, a newsletter inclusion, an Instagram Reel and a YouTube Short drawn from it, distributed through ADDD’s channels.
## What it needs from you
A real project or workflow, and a practice willing to take part. The sponsorship is disclosed in the episode itself.
items.lede: One episode built around a real architectural project or workflow: the people who did the work, how they did it, and where your technology fitted into it.

body: ## Where the insight comes from

ADDD works with practices on their technology decisions: reviewing workflows, untangling software estates and helping decide what to adopt, keep or replace. That work shows the problems, constraints and priorities behind their choices, which rarely appear in surveys or sales conversations.
## What a briefing covers

Each quarter’s briefing sets out what practices in your market category are doing, against a scope agreed at the start. It is measured by that scope and its regular delivery, not by conversion figures.
## How confidentiality is kept
Findings are anonymised. No practice is identified, and no raw data is shared.
items.lede: An ongoing intelligence relationship: every quarter, a briefing on what architecture practices in your category are doing, drawn from ADDD’s workshops and sessions with them.

body: ## When it fits

A newsletter placement suits a single, clear message, such as a launch, a useful resource or an event, rather than an ongoing presence. It reaches the architects and practice leaders who read ADDDitive alongside ADDD’s own writing on technology in practice.
## How it is handled
The placement is agreed on a first call: what it says, which issue it runs in and how it is linked. It is marked as a sponsored placement in the issue.

questions.answer: Anyone who shapes how work moves through the practice — a director or partner, the project lead for the chosen project, and whoever owns BIM, IT or operations. Between them they should be able to describe every stage of the project, from the brief to the last issue of drawings.
questions.question: Who should attend the workshop?

questions.answer: Between four and eight. Enough perspectives to see the whole flow, few enough that everyone contributes. If more people want a say, their views can be gathered through the questionnaire before the session.
questions.question: How many people should come?

questions.answer: A short questionnaire and the selection of one real project. Nothing else needs to be produced in advance: the session works from what the project already holds, and the questionnaire helps you choose one that shows the problems clearly.
questions.question: What preparation is required?

questions.answer: Yes. The workshop works because people are in the room together, working through a real project. Remote doesn’t create the same clarity. The session takes place at your office, so the team can bring the drawings, models and records it refers to.
questions.question: Does it have to be in person?

questions.answer: Within two weeks of the session. It sets out the findings, the priority areas and practical recommendations, and an optional readout can present them to your leadership.
questions.question: When do we get the report?

journey.heading: Workshop Process
journey.lede: Four stages, from a short questionnaire before the session to a written report and a clear place to start.

body: ## Choosing the project

Before the session, a short questionnaire helps you choose a project that exposed workflow problems or delays: one where deadlines slipped, information had to be chased or work was done twice. You also receive guidance on who should attend and how to prepare.

A good choice is recent enough that people remember it clearly and broad enough to have passed through several teams and tools. It does not need to be a troubled project, only a typical one: the patterns it shows are the ones every project shares.
## In the room

In the room, the project becomes a shared reference point. Rather than discussing workflows in the abstract, the team walks through what really happened, step by step, with the people who did the work.

Working from one project keeps the session concrete. Each stage is checked against what the project actually produced, the drawings, models, emails and meeting notes, so gaps show up as facts rather than opinions. Where people remember a stage differently, the difference itself is often the finding.
## What it gives you

Because every observation is tied to something the team can point at, the findings are hard to dismiss and easy to act on. The project also becomes a baseline: it can be revisited after changes are made, to see what has improved.
documents.lede: The workshop starts from a project your team has just delivered or is working on now. Because the evidence is your own, the findings describe how your practice actually works, not how a template says it should.
points: Findings grounded in your own work, not general advice
A shared reference everyone in the room recognises
Problems named precisely enough to act on
Evidence drawn from what the project actually produced

body: ## Seeing it all at once

Most practices already sense these problems; they rarely see them all at once, in context, or understand why they keep returning. The session separates symptoms from causes, so the conversation moves from frustration to specifics.
## Tracing the causes

Each friction point is traced back to where it starts: a missing standard, an unclear owner, a tool that does not pass information to the next, or a step that survives only out of habit. Small, frequent losses are counted alongside the visible crises, because together they usually cost the most.

Where it helps, the time involved is estimated with the team: how often a problem occurs, how long it takes each time and who it affects. Rough numbers are enough to show which issues are worth solving first.
## Agreeing what matters

The friction points are then prioritised together, so the team agrees which matter most before anything changes. The written report that follows within two weeks sets them out with practical recommendations and next steps.
documents.lede: With the project laid out, the workshop pinpoints where time is lost: the duplicated effort, the information that disappears between stages, the decisions nobody recorded and the responsibilities that blur.
points: A prioritised list of friction points, agreed by the team
The causes behind recurring delays, not just the symptoms
A clear starting point for change, without a larger commitment
Small, everyday losses counted alongside the visible ones

body: ## Drawing the flow

Mapping the actual flow shows where the handoffs are, which tools each stage depends on and where the same information is entered more than once. It makes the unseen parts of the process visible to everyone at the same time.

The map is drawn live, stage by stage: who does what, with which tools, and what passes to the next person. Loops, workarounds and waiting time are marked where they happen, so the team can see at a glance where the flow slows down or breaks.
## What the map reveals

Seen whole, the flow usually shows a few places where most of the trouble gathers: a stage that waits on another, a tool only one person fully understands, or an approval that holds everything up. These become the focus of the recommendations.
## Using it afterwards
The map becomes a shared picture the whole team can return to. It is the foundation for the findings, priorities and recommendations in the report, and a reference for any change that follows.
documents.lede: Over four hours, the team traces how information, decisions and work move through the practice, from brief to completion, and draws the flow as it really is, not as the process documents describe it.
points: One shared view of how work moves through the practice
Every handoff, tool and duplication made visible
A foundation for decisions about workflows and tools
Loops, workarounds and waiting time marked where they occur
